questions.question: Determine the equivalent point and concentration of Fe2_+ ions by potentiometric titration with standard potassium dichromate solution in an acidic medium.
questions.solution_html:
• electrode and reference electrode with suitable examples
  • Potentiometric titration is a volumetric method in which the potential difference between two electrodes is
  • measured as a function of the added titrant volume. The principle rests on the Nernst Equation, which
  • relates the electrode potential to the concentration of the species in the solution
  • Instrumentation- 3 main components
  • Reference Electrode: An electrode with a constant, known potential (e.g., Saturated Calomel Electrode or
  • Ag/AgCl electrode).
  • Indicator Electrode: An electrode whose potential depends on the concentration of the analyte (e.g., Glass
  • electrode for pH, Platinum wire for redox).
  • Potentiometer/pH Meter: To measure the potential difference between the two electrodes.
  • Working
  • The analyte solution is taken in a beaker.
  • The indicator electrode and reference electrode are immersed in the solution.
  • The titrant is added gradually from the burette.
  • After each addition, the potential difference (E) is measured.
  • A graph is plotted between: Potential (E) vs Volume of titrant, or ΔE/ΔV vs Volume (for sharper
  • endpoint detection).
  • The equivalence point is identified from the sharp jump in potential or peak in derivative curve.
  • Indicator electrode responds to the activity (concentration) of the analyte ion and reference electrode
  • maintains a constant potential regardless of solution composition. For example, in case of acid- base titration
  • indicator electrode is Glass electrode and reference electrode is Calomel electrode.
  • (Principle(2 marks), Instrumentation(3 marks), working (3 marks), Electrodes explanation(2 marks))
questions.final_answer: (Principle- , Instrumentation- , working - , Electrodes explanation

  • Cleansing action of soap
  • The way soap removes dirt and grease is a classic example of emulsification. Dirt is usually oily, and since
  • water and oil don't mix, water alone can’t be used to clean. A soap molecule has two distinct ends
  • Hydrophilic Head: Water-loving and polar and Hydrophobic Tail: Water-fearing and non-polar (usually a long
  • hydrocarbon chain). When we apply soap to greasy hands, the hydrophobic tails "dive" into the oil/grease
  • while the hydrophilic heads stay pointing out toward the water. The soap molecules surround the oil
  • droplet, forming a spherical structure called a micelle. The oil is trapped in the centre. As we scrub

  • is negatively charged (the heads), they repel each other. This prevents the oil droplets from clumping back
  • together.

questions.question: Explain the principle, instrumentation, and working of potentiometric titration. Discuss the role of indicator electrode and reference electrode with suitable examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Potentiometric titration is a volumetric method in which the potential difference between two electrodes is
  • measured as a function of the added titrant volume. The principle rests on the Nernst Equation, which
  • relates the electrode potential to the concentration of the species in the solution
  • Instrumentation- 3 main components
  • Reference Electrode: An electrode with a constant, known potential (e.g., Saturated Calomel Electrode or
  • Ag/AgCl electrode).
  • Indicator Electrode: An electrode whose potential depends on the concentration of the analyte (e.g., Glass
  • electrode for pH, Platinum wire for redox).
  • Potentiometer/pH Meter: To measure the potential difference between the two electrodes.
  • Working
  • The analyte solution is taken in a beaker.
  • The indicator electrode and reference electrode are immersed in the solution.
  • The titrant is added gradually from the burette.
  • After each addition, the potential difference (E) is measured.
  • A graph is plotted between: Potential (E) vs Volume of titrant, or ΔE/ΔV vs Volume (for sharper
  • endpoint detection).
  • The equivalence point is identified from the sharp jump in potential or peak in derivative curve.
  • Indicator electrode responds to the activity (concentration) of the analyte ion and reference electrode
  • maintains a constant potential regardless of solution composition. For example, in case of acid- base titration
  • (Principle(2 marks), Instrumentation(3 marks), working (3 marks), Electrodes explanation(2 marks))
